approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would change how travel entitlements for current and former parliamentarians work.

It would add a 25% loading on certain travel claim adjustments, cut the age limit for children's travel from 25 to 18, and rename the Life Gold Pass scheme to the Parliamentary Retirement Travel Entitlement.

From 14 May 2014, the bill would close the entitlement to people who had not met qualifying periods by that date, and from 1 January 2020, no one except former prime ministers could access the scheme.
Imposes a 25% loading on adjustments to certain travel claims.
Restricts the additional travel for children entitlement to children under 18 for senior officers.
Renames the Members of Parliament (Life Gold Pass) Act 2002 to the Parliamentary Retirement Travel Act 2002.
Reduces, removes, and reforms benefits under the Life Gold Pass scheme.
Adds a statutory basis for recovering payments made outside entitlement to address constitutional risks.
Current and former parliamentarians, their spouses or de facto partners, and senior officers.

Moved the Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill, which imposes a 25 per cent penalty loading for adjustments to MPs' travel claims and reduces the parliamentary retirement travel entitlement, known as the Life Gold Pass, including capping a former prime minister's travel to 30 return domestic trips a year.

Argued that Labor supports abolishing the gold pass in the Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill 2014 but wants it improved, opposing cuts to travel for former prime ministers and dependent children, and noting the bill sets former parliamentarians' post-service travel at 10 trips per year over six years despite the Remuneration Tribunal not having considered the change.

Argued in support of the Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, which reduces and eventually abolishes the life gold pass travel scheme for all but former prime ministers, noting the government's 15.4 per cent superannuation contribution for MPs and citing a $50 billion budget deficit and debt forecast to reach $667 billion without intervention.

Argued in support of the Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, emphasising that members of parliament must serve with integrity, honesty and transparency, and referred to the conduct of the former member for Corangamite before being ruled out of order.

Summed up the Parliamentary Entitlements Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, confirming it limits dependent children's travel entitlement to those under 18, imposes a 25 per cent penalty on adjusted travel claims, and sets post-service travel at 10 trips a year for six years for senior officeholders and 30 trips a year for life for former prime ministers.

Presented the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights' examination of the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (Foreign Fighters) Bill 2014, concluding that its declared area offence, carrying up to 10 years imprisonment, is likely incompatible with human rights because it reverses the presumption of innocence, and raised concerns about a new advocating terrorism offence that could criminalise speech through a recklessness test.

Sought the Speaker's guidance on whether standing order 90, which requires withdrawing remarks that impugn a member, applies to a comment about a dishonest campaign attributed to a former, rather than current, member for Corangamite.

A motion was moved requesting the Senate to resume consideration of 14 specified bills from the previous session, with each request to be conveyed in a separate message. The bills covered water amendment, managed investment trusts, social services, crime commission, deaths registration, tax and superannuation, crowd-sourced funding, firearms trafficking, and parliamentary entitlements.
